Compared to certain other instructors, taking GE301 from Robin Ann Downey requires a lot more effort. I get the sense that she sees this course as an opportunity to show the engineering students - that are stereotyped to be (not directly by her but by society in general) socially unaware, only technically minded people - the world of STS. Probably for this reason, the syllabus was full of STS literature. However, I can say that her effort missed the mark for me. In fact, after taking this course I have a great antipathy for STS. Not only did I become uninterested in the topic, but also the structure and the workload of this course was a terror on me in my third year.

For this course you need to do a project involving a field site. She requires the selection of the field site to be done on the second week without proper preparation and understanding of the requirements. However, almost everybody does their project on the last two weeks. So, this is not a real requirement and only causes problems. Moreover, throughout the project related meetings in the semester she has certain ideas that she pushes on your group. These ideas are generally very fundamental parts of your project such as the theoretical approach to take. She is very insistent about her ideas and because she is doing the grading you can not afford to go against her ideas in order to get a good grade.

Another major problem is the midterm exam. Every instructor prepares their own midterm and it has a weight of 35. Every question in her midterm was 3 to 5 questions of the type "What did this author say in that text?", "Define ideas described in that text." chained together. It rewarded memorization more than critical thinking. Had you memorized the texts and the lectures you did not even need to think, you could write down a bullet list and be done with the question. Critical thinking did not get you anywhere at all. Also, questions were very specific.

You are losing grades and time by choosing her.

There are two major problems with this course. First one is that it takes too much time. It is a must course for third years and at least IE and CS students have a lot of must courses with heavy workloads in the same semester. It is ridiculous that a 2 credit course would cause such pain and suffering for the students that are forced to take it. One major contributor to this is the group project of this course. It is worse than department specific courses' group projects. You are more likely to get terrible teammates that are disinterested, lazy or incompetent beyond belief.

The other problem is the lack of standardization. Every instructor teaches their own syllabus, prepares their own exams and are given freedom in how they conduct their course. Which instructor you get is just luck. It can be seen from statistics and past evaluations that some instructors are simply better than others from the perspective of a student. They give better grades and less work. It is ironic for a course all about ethics and values to cause such an injustice among students. If every student was taught the same material and was given the same exam at least it would be fair.

Strong aspects: Andrew Feenberg's ideas were interesting.
Weak aspects: I don't think I gained much from this course aside from more anxiety regarding the term project. If this course only consisted of the readings and the discussions, I probably wouldn't be this negative about it, but I don't think this course is doing what ABET wants it to do. I don't think anyone gains anything (especially as a junior engineering student) from the interviews and from preparing the project. The interviews require you to already have connections in the software engineering industry with people willing to allocate time to discuss their company. It is technically possible to complete the term project without interviews, but it requires you to collect a lot more academic sources compared to groups that do interviews, and you have general news articles instead of questions specifically prepared for the STS context to derive your argument from. The reading material did have some interesting ideas from time to time, but it is likely that you will end up cringing when you see a bicycle after this course. And also you can't use the later (and, in my opinion, much more interesting) readings meaningfully when constructing an argument for your term project, which makes them seem less important. If the course went under a major overhaul and reconstructed more like the humanities courses, the in-class discussions and the ideas about technology and society could lead to a more fruitful and engaging course. However, in its current state, this course consists of anxiety-inducing busywork which is unfortunate for a course supposed to introduce new perspectives to prospective engineers.
